context_blurb:
Every cell in your body runs on a slow, controlled burning: sugar and the oxygen you breathe become water and carbon dioxide, freeing the energy behind every heartbeat. Enzymes, the cell's protein tools, run each reaction along the way.

Antoine Lavoisier thought breathing burns carbon slowly, as a fire does. Around 1783 he and Pierre-Simon Laplace weighed the ice a guinea pig's heat melted. Fast or slow, burning carbon gives the same heat, so the fair test is heat for each ounce of fixed air, our carbon dioxide. The animal melted 13 ounces where charcoal making as much fixed air melts about 10: near enough as much ice for each ounce of fixed air as burning charcoal melts.

That slow burning is cellular respiration, which stores its energy in ATP (adenosine triphosphate), a small molecule cells spend like coins, made mostly in the mitochondria. At the end of a reaction chain on their inner membrane, oxygen takes up electrons and hydrogen ions, ending up in the water made in the mitochondria. The carbon dioxide you breathe out comes from the sugar's own carbon.

In the mid-1930s Albert Szent-Györgyi found that traces of succinate or fumarate, acids cells make, sped minced pigeon muscle's oxygen use far beyond what so little acid could fuel. In 1937 Hans Krebs and William Johnson saw citrate do the same. Krebs reasoned that each is used up by one reaction and remade by a later one, at the end of a loop of reactions. This Krebs cycle frees carbon dioxide at each turn.

Without oxygen, cells fall back on fermentation, running only the first steps of breaking down sugar for 2 ATP per glucose, against many times more with oxygen. Around 1860 Louis Pasteur spread yeast thin in a dish open to the air, and it multiplied faster and fermented less. Sealed away from air, it fermented hard, spending far more sugar on each gram of new yeast. Each sugar yields far less ATP without oxygen, so sealed yeast needs far more sugar to grow as much.

Muscle short of oxygen in a hard run ferments too, making lactic acid, or lactate, once wrongly blamed for next-day soreness. But blood lactate is back to normal within about an hour, long before the ache peaks one to three days later. Tiny tears in muscle fibres, mostly where muscles lengthen as they pull, are thought to cause it: in a 1983 test, an easier downhill run left legs sore, a harder level run did not.

An enzyme is a molecule, nearly always a protein, that speeds a reaction and comes out unchanged. Dry glucose sits unchanged on a shelf, though it burns fiercely, because every reaction needs a push to start: its activation energy. An enzyme lowers the energy needed to start its step, offering an easier path, so the step runs millions of times faster at body heat.

Pasteur's followers held that only a living cell ferments. In 1897 Eduard Buchner pressed juice from yeast crushed with sand; given cane sugar, it bubbled out carbon dioxide for days. Yet stray living cells might explain that. The deciding test was a filter that holds back every cell: had the juice, filtered of all its yeast cells, not fermented, Buchner would have been wrong. It fermented: a dissolved substance, zymase, did the work.

In 1926 James Sumner crystallised urease, from jack beans, and found it was protein. Richard Willstätter said the protein was only a carrier for the real enzyme, a far smaller molecule. John Northrop recrystallised pepsin, a stomach enzyme, over and over. A clinging molecule should have been shed bit by bit, yet each gram kept the same activity through seven crystallisations, so pepsin itself is a protein.

Each enzyme acts on its own substrate, the molecule it works on. Methyl glucoside comes in two forms of the same atoms, differing only in which way one group points. In 1894 Emil Fischer found that a yeast enzyme split one form and emulsin, an almond enzyme, only the other. Fischer explained that only the matching form fitted each enzyme's own shape, as a key fits its lock.

Heat can ruin that shape. A moderate fever is a rise the brain sets on purpose, thought to help fight infection; heat stroke is the body's heat control failing. Above about 40 degrees Celsius proteins begin to unfold, and in a body held at 42 or more, enzymes lose the shape their work depends on, so cells and organs fail.
